Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

Because the narrative spans over a year of slow institutional and structural decay (along with fifty-four years of architectural history), the author effectively uses summary and exposition to compress time, provide background on the building, and show the gradual fracturing of the academic department across months. However, to prevent the story from feeling dry or detached, the author anchors each section with brief, vivid scenes unfolding in real-time—such as the October faculty meeting, Helen's dryly humorous conversation with Tomasz about the plastic-covered windows, and the final, tactile scene on the scaffolding where Helen actually touches the newly installed membrane. This balance allows the story to cover a long timeline while remaining emotionally resonant and grounded in character interaction.
